title: A shabad for your home
hookLine: many families have a shabad they keep for their house

lines: A FRAMED LINE BY THE DOOR.
cards: In some Sikh homes, the shabad is on the wall before anyone sings it: a framed line of Gurmukhi by the front door, or above the stove, or in the hallway. Ask about it, and you'll often get a story.
It was my grandmother's favorite. My dad sang it when we moved from Kenya. We played it the night the baby came home.
Families have songs the way they have recipes, passed down without anyone deciding to. In some Sikh households, one of those songs is a shabad.

teach.b: Shabad means word, and in Sikh life it means a hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word sung.

teach.h: HOW A FAMILY GETS ITS HYMN.
teach.b: There's no rule that a family must have one shabad of its own. But some do, and it happens in ordinary ways.
A house is blessed with a reading of Sukhmani Sahib and an Ardas when a family moves in, and one line from that day sticks.
A grandmother hums the same hymn every evening for years, and her grandchildren hum it without knowing the words. A parent sings one to a child at bedtime, and it becomes theirs.

teach.h: DUKH BHANJAN: YOUR NAME ENDS PAIN.
teach.b: Some keep a well-loved line like dukh bhanjan teraa naam: Your Name destroys pain.
That shabad of Guru Arjan, on Ang two eighteen, goes on: dwell on it through all the hours of the day; this is the perfect True Guru's wisdom.
Others choose taatee vaao na lagaee, the hot wind that doesn't touch, or the Anand Sahib's opening joy. Why does it matter?

teach.h: THE WORD LIVES WHERE YOU LIVE.
teach.b: A household shabad works like a family's memory. It's there at the birthday and at the hospital, sung in the car and over the dishes. When something hard happens, nobody has to search for words.
The words are already in the house, worn smooth by use. And underneath is a Sikh idea: the Guru isn't kept only in the gurdwara.
The Word can live where you live, in the kitchen and the hallway, sung by people in their socks.

how: Some Sikh families keep a favorite shabad for their home: framed by the door, sung at bedtime or on family occasions, often first heard at a house blessing with Sukhmani Sahib and Ardas.

o: a cure from a village healer
pain the body must simply bear

games.q: a shabad for your home — tap the pairs.

s: Sikh rules require every family to have its own shabad
there's no rule; many families simply come to have one.
dukh bhanjan teraa naam is a shabad of Guru Arjan
on Ang 218: Your Name destroys pain.

games.q: your family just moved into a new house. how do Sikh families often bless it?
o: with a reading of Sukhmani Sahib and an Ardas.
by keeping the house silent for a week.
games.why: families often mark a new home with Sukhmani Sahib and Ardas, and a line from that day may become theirs.

practice: Think back over the lines you've met on this path, a line from the laavan, the hot wind, the Name that ends pain, and ask which one you'd want in your house: by the door, at bedtime, on a hard day.
Let one rise, and say its words or its meaning silently, as if in your own kitchen. If you pray, say Waheguru after it.

wordCard.voice: Dukh bhanjan, destroyer of pain: one well-loved line families keep, like dukh bhanjan teraa naam, sung at birthdays and hospital beds, passed down like a recipe, so the words are already there when they're needed.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: word; in Sikh life, a hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: our shabad. The words can be in the house before they're needed. See you tomorrow.
